title: Mixed Precision Training ⚡
description: Speed up training and reduce memory with torch.cuda.amp and GradScaler.

slides.title: Why Mixed Precision? 🏎️
slides.content:
# Float16 Speed, Float32 Stability

Modern GPUs (Volta+) have **Tensor Cores** that accelerate FP16 matrix multiplies. But pure FP16 can cause gradient underflow/loss of precision.

**Mixed precision** uses:
* FP16 for forward/backward convolutions.
* FP32 for master weights and reductions.

PyTorch provides `torch.cuda.amp` to automate this.

slides.title: Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP)
slides.codeSnippet:
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()

for data, target in train_loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
        output = model(data.cuda())
        loss = criterion(output, target.cuda())
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()

quizData.question: What is the role of `GradScaler`?

options.text: It scales loss up to prevent gradients from underflowing in FP16

quizData.explanation: GradScaler multiplies loss by a large factor so small gradients in FP16 don't vanish.

slides.title: How AMP Works 🧪
slides.content:
## Inside `autocast`

`autocast` context manager casts eligible operations (linear, conv, matmul) to FP16 automatically. Operations unsafe in FP16 (softmax, loss) stay FP32.

GradScaler dynamically adjusts the loss scale: if gradients overflow, it skips the step and reduces scale; otherwise, increases scale gradually.

slides.content: Compare memory with and without AMP.
slides.codeSnippet:

quizData.question: Which operations typically stay in FP32 under autocast?
quizData.explanation: Softmax, losses, and other numerically sensitive ops remain in FP32 for stability.
